lead: Four things decide how a journal bearing behaves: shaft speed, oil viscosity, load and clearance. Change one and the film thickness, friction and oil flow all move. The Sommerfeld number packs all four into a single dimensionless group, so one set of charts can describe every bearing of a given length-to-diameter ratio. It is the number you look up on the Raimondi and Boyd charts, the number you quote when comparing two bearing designs, and the quickest check on whether a bearing is running with a safe oil film or is about to rub.
prereq: You need: the oil-film picture of a hydrodynamic journal bearing from Chapter 5.3, and viscosity and its units from Chapter 5.1.

blocks.text: Speed, viscosity, load and clearance act together. Charts drawn against four separate variables would need a library of curves, one for every size and every oil. That is unworkable in a design office.

Dimensional analysis removes the size and the units. The group μn/p has no dimensions: (Pa·s × 1/s) ÷ Pa leaves nothing. The group r/c has none either, because both are lengths in metres. Combine them and one number carries the effect of speed, viscosity, load and clearance at once.

Two bearings with the same value of that number and the same length-to-diameter ratio behave alike, even if one is a 25 mm pump shaft and the other a 250 mm turbine shaft. A four-variable problem becomes a one-variable problem, and a single chart covers every bearing of a given L/D.

blocks.where: S is the Sommerfeld number, dimensionless. μ is the dynamic viscosity of the oil at its working temperature, in Pa·s. n is shaft speed in revolutions per second (rev/s). p is the bearing pressure in Pa, p = W/(L D), where W is the load in N, L is the bearing length in m and D is the journal diameter in m. r is the journal radius in m, r = D/2. c is the radial clearance in m, the gap on one side.

blocks.text: Substituting p = W/(L D) removes the pressure and gives the form used when you know the load directly:
S = μ n L D (r/c)² / W
blocks.where: the symbols are as above; μn is a pressure (Pa), so μn × LD/W is (pressure × area)/force, a pure number. S stays dimensionless whatever units you use, as long as you are consistent.

blocks.text: Some books call the group μn/p the bearing characteristic number or bearing modulus. The Sommerfeld number is that group multiplied by (r/c)². Keep the two names apart.

The ratio r/c sits inside a square, so it dominates. For a machined bearing r/c typically lies between 500 and 1000 (c/r = 0.001 to 0.002). At r/c = 500 the square is 250 000, which is why S usually lands between 0.01 and 1 even though μn/p is of the order of 10⁻⁷.
A few books print 1/S under the same name. Before reading any chart, check which way its curves run.

sections.h3: What a high or low S means

blocks.text: Eccentricity e is the offset of the journal centre from the bush centre; the eccentricity ratio is ε = e/c, and the minimum film thickness is h₀ = c(1 − ε). High S means small ε and a thick film.

items: S rises in direct proportion to viscosity μ and to speed n.
S falls as load W rises, and falls as the square of the clearance c grows.
Small S: the journal is pushed close to the bush, the minimum film is thin, and the risk of metal-to-metal contact and wear is high.
Large S: the journal floats higher, eccentricity falls and the film thickens, but the film shears more oil and generates more heat to be carried away.

blocks.text: The design aim is a middle band. Very small S gives a thin, hot, wearing bearing; very large S wastes power in churning viscous oil. For the same L/D, a bearing running at higher S generally sits at lower eccentricity, so the same eccentricity chart serves every size once you plot against S.

This is why the Sommerfeld number is the horizontal axis of the design charts in Chapter 5.5. You compute S, follow it up to the curve for your L/D, and read eccentricity, minimum film thickness, friction and oil flow.
Three inputs cause most of the lost marks.

items: Speed: use revolutions per second. A shaft at 1500 rpm is at 25 rev/s, not 1500.
Pressure: use the projected area L × D. The oil film pressure acts on the projected rectangle of the journal, not on the curved surface πDL.
Viscosity: use the value at the oil's operating temperature inside the bearing, not the ISO VG grade number or the value at 40 °C from a supplier table.

blocks.text: Clearance is radial: c = (bush bore − journal diameter)/2. Using the diametral clearance halves the ratio r/c and quarters S. Keep every length in metres and every pressure in pascals and the group stays dimensionless.

figure.caption: The load of the worked example spreads over the projected rectangle L × D, not over the curved surface. That gives p = 4 MPa and S = 0.03125; using πDL would make S look π times larger and the film safer than it is.

examples.question: A full journal bearing carries a steady load W = 10 kN. Journal diameter D = 50 mm, bearing length L = 50 mm, radial clearance c = 0.05 mm. The shaft runs at 1500 rpm and the oil viscosity at the working temperature is μ = 0.02 Pa·s. Calculate the Sommerfeld number.
steps: Convert the speed to revolutions per second: n = 1500/60 = 25 rev/s.
Journal radius: r = D/2 = 0.050/2 = 0.025 m. Radial clearance: c = 0.05 mm = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m.
Bearing pressure: p = W/(L D) = 10 000/(2.5 × 10⁻³) = 4 × 10⁶ Pa = 4 MPa.
examples.answer: The Sommerfeld number is S = 0.03125, dimensionless.

traps: Putting n in rpm. The group needs revolutions per second; 1500 rpm is 25 rev/s, and using 1500 inflates S sixty times.

Using πDL as the area. Bearing pressure acts on the projected area L × D, the rectangle you see when you look at the bearing from the side; πDL is the curved surface of the journal and makes p π times too small.
Feeding in the diametral clearance instead of the radial clearance. That halves r/c and cuts S to one quarter.
Forgetting to square r/c. The ratio is around 500, so dropping the square changes S by a factor of 250 000.
Taking viscosity at 40 °C from a grade table. The bearing runs hotter and thinner; S must use the viscosity at the operating temperature.

quiz.q: Write the Sommerfeld number and state the unit of each quantity in it.
quiz.a: S = (μn/p)(r/c)², dimensionless. μ in Pa·s, n in rev/s, p in Pa, r and c in m.

quiz.q: Explain why the Sommerfeld number is dimensionless and why that matters for bearing design.
quiz.a: μn/p is (Pa·s)(1/s)/(Pa), which cancels to a pure number, and r/c is a ratio of two lengths. Being dimensionless, S keeps the same value if you switch from metres to millimetres, so one chart serves bearings of every size.

quiz.q: A bearing has μ = 0.03 Pa·s, n = 20 rev/s, p = 2 MPa and r/c = 800. Find S.
W = 5 kN, D = 40 mm, L = 40 mm, c = 0.04 mm, n = 3000 rpm, μ = 0.015 Pa·s. Find S.
The speed of a bearing doubles while the load, oil and clearance stay the same. What happens to S and to the eccentricity?
quiz.a: S is proportional to n, so it doubles. A higher S at the same L/D means the journal rides higher and the eccentricity ratio falls, giving a thicker minimum film.

quiz.q: A student computes p using πDL instead of LD. By what factor does the calculated S differ from the correct value, and is the error safe or unsafe?
quiz.a: Using πDL makes the area larger by π, so p is smaller by π and S becomes π times too large, about 3.14 times. A larger S suggests a thicker film than reality, so the error is unsafe: it hides a thin-film risk.

quiz.q: Why does r/c dominate the value of S more than μ or n?
quiz.a: Because r/c is around 500 and is squared, contributing about 2.5 × 10⁵, while μn/p is of order 10⁻⁷. Small changes in clearance therefore swing S far more than the same percentage change in speed or viscosity.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the Sommerfeld number is the bridge between a quick hand calculation and a full thermo-hydrodynamic simulation; commercial bearing codes still report it alongside eccentricity so results can be compared with the classical charts. Research on turbulent and misaligned bearings keeps the same group but adds correction factors for Reynolds number and tilt. Search next for the Raimondi and Boyd charts, the Reynolds equation for the oil film, and the Ocvirk short-bearing approximation, which handles bearings with small L/D where the classical charts lose accuracy.
